<description>
{
 "summary": "Stops the internal HTTP server from reading or executing subsequent requests pipelined behind a \"Connection: close\" request. The server records when a closing reply has been queued or a disconnection has been flagged, preventing queued bytes in the receive buffer from being handed to RPC workers.",
 "problem": "Following the custom HTTP server implementation in #35182, the server still parses remaining bytes in the receive buffer after queuing a close reply, executing pipelined requests whose replies are then dropped upon client disconnection. If an RPC client adheres to RFC 9112 section 9.6 and resends requests that received no response on a closed connection, RPC methods with side effects can execute twice.",
 "evidence": [
  "RFC 9112 section 9.6 requires a server that sends a close response not to process any further requests on that connection.",
  "Description notes this is a regression from #35182: \"The libevent based server freed the connection right after writing the close reply (evhttp_send_done() \u2192 evhttp_connection_free()), discarding any pipelined bytes\"."
 ],

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.
